name: Intralobar Congenital Pulmonary Sequestration

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Radiologic and Surgical Diagnostic Criteria for Pulmonary Sequestration

criteria.description: Presence of aberrant systemic arterial supply to a non-functioning segment of lung
Lack of normal connection between the sequestered lung tissue and the tracheobronchial tree
Sequestered lung tissue located within the visceral pleura of a normal lobe (intralobar)
Identification of sequestered lung tissue and aberrant vessels on CT angiography or MRI
Histopathological confirmation of non-functioning lung tissue without normal bronchial connections

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of aberrant systemic arterial supply and intralobar location with absence of normal bronchial connection confirmed by imaging or surgery
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is often confirmed intraoperatively or by advanced imaging techniques such as CT angiography.

pathognomonic.notes: Repeated infections localized to the affected lung segment
searchTerms: repeated lung infections in same area

pathognomonic.symptomName: Chronic productive cough with purulent sputum
searchTerms: cough with yellow or green mucus

pathognomonic.symptomName: Hemoptysis originating from sequestered lung tissue
pathognomonic.notes: Coughing up blood due to abnormal vasculature
searchTerms: coughing up blood from lung lesion
hemoptysis due to abnormal lung tissue

common.symptomName: Chest discomfort or localized chest pain
Wheezing localized to affected lung area
searchTerms: wheezing sound in affected lung area

occasional.symptomName: Weight loss associated with chronic infection
searchTerms: losing weight due to long-term infection

occasional.symptomName: Fatigue related to chronic pulmonary disease

rare.notes: Secondary to chronic hypoxia or shunting

laboratory: Elevated inflammatory markers during infection (e.g., ESR, CRP)
Possible leukocytosis during acute infection episodes
imaging: CT angiography showing aberrant systemic arterial supply to sequestered lung segment
Chest X-ray revealing localized opacity or cystic lesion
MRI demonstrating non-functioning lung tissue without bronchial connection
genetic: No specific genetic mutations identified; considered sporadic congenital malformation
other: Surgical findings of sequestered lung tissue within visceral pleura
Histopathology confirming non-functioning lung parenchyma without normal bronchial connections

distinguishingFeatures: Sequestered lung tissue located outside visceral pleura
More common in infants and associated with other congenital anomalies
Diffuse bronchial dilation involving multiple lobes
Usually secondary to infection or obstruction
Presence of cystic lung lesions communicating with bronchial tree
Usually diagnosed in neonates or infants

redFlags: Recurrent severe pulmonary infections unresponsive to antibiotics
references: Savic B, Birtel FJ, Tholen W, Funke HD, Knoche R. Lung sequestration: report of seven cases and review of 540 published cases. Thorax. 1979;34(1):96-101.
Corbett HJ, Humphrey GM. Pulmonary sequestration. Paediatric Respiratory Reviews. 2004;5(1):59-68.
Stocker JT. Congenital pulmonary airway malformation: a new name for and an expanded classification of congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation of the lung. Histopathology. 2002;41(2):424-431.
